strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution. The central idea—using multimodal panoramic renderings as a 2D–3D interface for a pretrained VLM—is intuitive, technically relevant, and reasonably original. It preserves scene-wide relational context while avoiding orientation selection for conventional views.

The method is technically coherent: structure-aware viewpoint placement, semantic and range feature adapters, VLM-based 2D grounding, and visibility-aware lifting form a plausible end-to-end pipeline. Supporting both meshes and 3D Gaussian Splatting broadens its applicability.

The empirical results are strong. PanoGrounder substantially improves Nr3D accuracy (74.6 versus 69.9 for the strongest listed single-dataset baseline), achieves the best reported ScanRefer overall result, and remains competitive on Sr3D.

The paper evaluates more than in-distribution benchmark accuracy. Cross-dataset tests on ARKitScenes and 3RScan, multiple language perturbations, mesh-versus-3DGS experiments, camera-placement studies, modality/objective ablations, qualitative examples, and runtime measurements provide broad supporting evidence.

The panorama-versus-pinhole analysis supports the main representational claim, particularly for descriptions involving several contextual objects. The camera-placement ablation also shows that comparable accuracy can be obtained with substantially fewer viewpoints than random placement.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, and the supplement provides useful implementation details, prompts, convergence plots, and additional ablations.
weaknesses: The strongest generalization experiments do not evaluate the complete one-stage pipeline: Tables 2 and 3 use ground-truth object segmentations, and some baselines additionally use ground-truth semantic labels. These experiments demonstrate cross-domain candidate selection more clearly than end-to-end 3D localization, so the paper overstates the scope of the generalization conclusion.

The decimal digit-wise EMD loss is only an imperfect proxy for numerical box-coordinate distance. Independent place-weighted digit penalties behave poorly across carries (for example, nearby coordinates such as 199 and 200 differ in every digit), undermining the claimed numerical-order rationale. The ablation shows a modest benefit but does not compare against direct coordinate regression, ordinal tokenization, or a loss defined over the complete coordinate value.

Several important details of the 3D aggregation stage are underspecified, including the point-set denoising algorithm and thresholds, the precise SAM configuration and prompting, and behavior when masks or cross-view predictions fail. LoRA module selection and some adapter details are also missing, limiting exact reproducibility.

The panorama-versus-pinhole comparison is not fully controlled for total VLM evaluations, rendered angular resolution, or computation. PanoGrounder uses multiple cameras and four yaw-shifted test-time augmentations, while the accounting for corresponding pinhole inference budgets is unclear. Thus, Table 4 supports the usefulness of the full configuration but does not isolate panorama representation as cleanly as claimed.

Several reported gains are small—about one point on ScanRefer and less than one point for some objective ablations—but results are presented without multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance analysis. This makes it difficult to distinguish modest component gains from training variance.

The text-robustness sets are generated automatically by LLaMA without reported human validation. In particular, affordance rewriting may alter meaning, introduce stereotyped class cues, or fail to preserve all relational constraints, so the large gains on Affordance-no-name and Masked variants need dataset-quality auditing.

The practical-cost analysis excludes camera placement, multimodal panorama rendering, construction of the scene-level semantic field, and associated storage. Reporting only the 3.30-second online query time understates the complete deployment cost, especially for changing or newly reconstructed scenes.

The method assumes a high-quality renderable reconstruction, calibrated source views, and usually a capture trajectory; performance declines with 3DGS artifacts. These are meaningful applicability constraints that receive less attention than unsupported future directions about no-target, multi-target, and multitask operation.

strengths: The panoramic 2D–3D interface is an intuitive and practically relevant systems idea: it gives a pretrained VLM broad scene context while retaining a route back to metric 3D predictions.

The reported standard-benchmark results are strong. Under single-dataset training, the method reaches 74.6 on Nr3D and 61.0 Acc@0.25 on ScanRefer, exceeding the listed prior methods; mixed training raises these to 76.1 and 62.0.

The evaluation is broader than a benchmark-only study, including cross-dataset transfer, synthetic linguistic perturbations, panorama-versus-pinhole comparisons, camera-placement analysis, mesh/3DGS variants, runtime, and component ablations.

The paper is generally clear and visually polished. The three-stage pipeline, feature adapters, and training procedure are presented in an understandable way, and the supplementary material supplies several useful implementation details.
weaknesses: I assess this as an Algorithms/General submission, although much of the contribution is systems integration rather than a fundamentally new algorithm. The individual ingredients—panoramic rendering, DINO features, adapters, SAM-based lifting, multi-view consistency, and LoRA tuning of a large VLM—are largely established, making the originality of the technical components modest.

The strongest generalization claims rely on ground-truth object segmentations. In Tables 2 and 3, the predicted 2D box is matched against projected ground-truth instance masks, substantially simplifying localization and removing proposal and reconstruction errors. These results therefore demonstrate selection among oracle candidates, not general end-to-end 3D grounding on unseen datasets; the conclusion overstates them as evidence for generalizable open-vocabulary grounding.

The text-robustness study uses automatically generated LLaMA-3.3 variants without human verification or reporting how often meaning, relations, or target identity are preserved. Affordance rewrites can inject model-generated category cues, while noun masking can create unnatural expressions. Without annotation-quality measurements or evaluation on independently collected language, the large gains do not convincingly establish linguistic reasoning.

The proposed “EMD” loss is not a true distance between the represented coordinates: it separately penalizes decimal digits with place-value weights. Carry boundaries make adjacent values such as 099 and 100 appear very distant, whereas some larger coordinate errors can receive misleading decomposed penalties. The paper neither discusses this defect nor compares against direct coordinate regression, ordinal losses, or a Wasserstein loss over complete coordinate bins.

Several essential inference details are insufficiently specified, including the exact SAM variant and prompting/output-selection procedure, the point-cloud “denoising” operation and thresholds, seam-crossing boxes in equirectangular panoramas, and failure handling when the target is invisible. These omissions affect the final 3D boxes and impede reproducibility.

The ablations do not convincingly isolate the claimed geometric contributions. Adding geometry alone reduces accuracy from 60.4 to 60.2, and the complete geometry-plus-QA configuration improves over semantic features plus QA by only 0.3 points. No uncertainty or repeated-run variation is reported, so the claimed synergy may be within noise.

Comparisons are difficult to interpret computationally: the method fine-tunes a 17B-parameter CogVLM, uses a trainable DINOv2 geometry encoder, precomputes a multi-view semantic field from original RGB frames and camera poses, and performs about 9.6 VLM passes per query. Model sizes, training cost, preprocessing cost, and controlled comparisons to similarly scaled baselines are missing, weakening claims of simplicity and efficiency.

The panorama-versus-pinhole comparison is potentially confounded by input information, augmentation, and compute. The manuscript does not establish that the pinhole baselines receive comparable pixel budgets, training treatment, multi-view fusion, or numbers of VLM forward passes. Thus Table 4 does not by itself show that panoramas are intrinsically superior.

The stated limitations omit important practical restrictions: dependence on a high-quality renderable reconstruction, known poses and capture imagery for semantic lifting, sensitivity to reconstruction artifacts, high memory/compute cost, and restriction to single present targets. Overall, the promising empirical results merit attention, but the oracle-assisted generalization evidence, under-specified pipeline, and insufficient controls leave the central claims short of acceptance.

strengths: The panoramic 2D–3D interface is a clear, practically motivated contribution: it preserves scene-wide relational context while allowing a pretrained 2D VLM to be used with comparatively lightweight adaptation.

The method is technically coherent, combining structure-aware viewpoint placement, semantic and range features, VLM-based 2D grounding, and visibility-aware lifting into a complete 3D grounding pipeline.

Results are strong across several established benchmarks. Under single-dataset training, the method reaches 74.6% on Nr3D and 61.0% Acc@0.25 on ScanRefer, exceeding the reported comparison methods; mixed training improves these to 76.1% and 62.0%.

The evaluation is unusually broad: it includes cross-dataset transfer to ARKitScenes and 3RScan, multiple linguistic perturbations, panorama-versus-pinhole comparisons, mesh-versus-3DGS experiments, component ablations, camera-placement studies, qualitative results, and runtime measurements.

The gains on language variants without explicit target nouns are compelling: the method exceeds PQ3D by 15.9 points on the no-name affordance variant and by 8.5 points on masked queries, supporting the motivation for leveraging a strong VLM.

Ablations generally support the design choices. In particular, the panoramic representation substantially outperforms non-oracle pinhole configurations, and structure-aware placement attains comparable accuracy to roughly seven random cameras using only 2.4 cameras per scene.

The paper is well organized and visually clear, with an intuitive pipeline and sufficiently detailed supplementary material. weaknesses: The ScanRefer evaluation reports only Acc@0.25, omitting the commonly reported Acc@0.5 metric. Because the method converts SAM masks and depth samples into fitted 3D boxes, the stricter metric is important for establishing localization precision and substantiating the state-of-the-art claim.

The stated input assumption is incomplete. Although the method is presented as requiring a renderable 3D representation, its strongest configuration additionally needs the original RGB views, calibrated camera poses, and reconstruction trajectory to construct the semantic field and camera-placement score. Applicability when these resources are unavailable is not evaluated.

Several implementation-critical details remain underspecified, including the denoising operation in 3D aggregation, the SAM variant and prompting settings, adapter dimensions and precise injection layers, failure handling for invalid VLM boxes, and preprocessing cost. These omissions weaken reproducibility.

The claimed efficiency should be qualified: inference uses a 17B-parameter VLM and averages 9.6 forward passes per query, taking 3.30 seconds on an A100. The reported runtime also excludes semantic-field construction, camera placement, and panorama rendering, so it does not characterize total deployment cost.

The digit-wise EMD formulation is not a faithful distance between complete coordinates because independent place-value penalties mishandle carries—for example, 099 and 100 are numerically adjacent but incur a large digit-wise cost. Its empirical gain is useful, but the paper's numerical-distance interpretation is overstated.

The language-generalization sets are generated by a single LLaMA model without reported human validation, generation-quality statistics, or checks for altered constraints and residual target-name leakage. Compatibility between generated phrasing and the pretrained VLM may also favor PanoGrounder relative to the non-VLM baselines.

The conclusion describes the system as open-vocabulary, but the experiments primarily use closed benchmark categories and linguistic rewrites of existing queries; there is no explicit unseen-category evaluation supporting that claim.

The limitations section is narrow. It does not discuss failures from panorama seams and distortion, reconstruction artifacts, missing capture trajectories, SAM errors, or the dependence on static indoor scenes. Statistical variability is also absent despite some headline improvements being approximately one percentage point.

strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution, the central idea—using a small set of panoramic renderings as a 2D–3D interface for a pretrained VLM—is intuitive, technically relevant, and reasonably original. It addresses the restricted context of perspective views while avoiding a bespoke 3D-language backbone.

The empirical results are strong. Under single-dataset training, the method reports 74.6% overall accuracy on Nr3D versus 69.9% for ViewSRD, and 61.0 Acc@0.25 on ScanRefer versus 60.0 for VGMamba. Joint training further raises these results to 76.1% and 62.0%, respectively.

The evaluation is unusually broad: it covers ScanRefer, Nr3D, Sr3D, zero-shot grounding, transfer to ARKitScenes and 3RScan, language perturbations, mesh versus 3DGS representations, backbone scaling, and a self-captured scene. Cross-dataset improvements are particularly substantial—for example, 53.5% on ARKitScenes compared with 36.1% for the strongest reported baseline.

The paper provides useful ablations for modalities, EMD supervision, geometric QA, camera placement, test-time rotations, adapter initialization and placement, and panorama-versus-pinhole inputs. Table 6 supports the central panoramic-context hypothesis, especially for descriptions mentioning several objects.

The supplementary material reports resource use, preprocessing cost, model hyperparameters, prompts, and failure cases. The discussion appropriately acknowledges reconstruction sensitivity, latency, ambiguity, occlusion, and partial localization.
weaknesses: The practical-input claims are stronger than the primary evidence supports. All main benchmark results use human-cleaned ScanNet meshes and known camera parameters, while semantic-feature construction additionally lifts features from calibrated original RGB views. The fully automated COLMAP+3DGS experiment excludes 49 of 141 validation scenes because reconstruction fails and drops to 55.1% on the retained subset; the self-captured evaluation contains only one scene and two qualitative queries.

Several important components lack controlled ablations. In particular, there is no isolation of visibility-aware 3D aggregation against simpler voting/fusion, SAM-based masks against box lifting, or the effect of excluding target-invisible views during training while necessarily encountering such views at inference. These omissions make it difficult to attribute the full improvement to the claimed components.

The coordinate loss is described as distance-aware EMD, but it is applied independently to decimal digits with place-value weights. This is not a faithful metric over the represented coordinate because carries create discontinuities—for example, adjacent values 099 and 100 can incur a much larger penalty than more distant values sharing leading digits. The modest empirical gain supports its utility as an auxiliary regularizer, but not the stronger numerical-distance interpretation.

The panoramic box formulation does not discuss the periodic image seam. Objects crossing the left/right boundary can produce an almost full-width tight box, and the four circular-shift test-time views make this issue directly relevant. A seam-aware box representation or quantitative analysis is needed. The use of a square 490×490 image for a 360°×180° equirectangular panorama also introduces nonstandard aspect distortion without analysis.

The panorama-versus-pinhole experiment is directionally useful but does not fully establish a representation-only advantage: view counts, visible pixels, augmentation, and inference budgets are not normalized clearly. Likewise, the zero-shot configuration is underspecified—particularly whether the learned adapters, semantic/geometric inputs, or other trained components are disabled—so Table 2 is difficult to reproduce and compare confidently.

The closest render-based VLM work, LIFT-GS, is cited and compared only in the supplement but is not substantively discussed in the related-work section. The manuscript should clarify the conceptual and experimental distinction from render-supervised 2D-to-3D grounding more directly.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive supplement: no code-release statement is provided, and details such as LoRA target modules, adapter hidden dimensions, SAM checkpoint/configuration, statistical-outlier-removal parameters, random seeds, and variability across runs are absent. Most reported gains have no confidence intervals, including several sub-point ablation differences.

strengths: The panoramic 2D–3D interface is a sensible and moderately original design: it preserves broad scene context while allowing reuse of pretrained 2D VLMs. The camera-placement, multimodal adapter, and cross-view lifting components form a coherent end-to-end system.

The reported benchmark results are strong. In the single-dataset setting, the method reaches 74.6 on Nr3D and 61.0 Acc@0.25 on ScanRefer, with particularly meaningful gains on relationally difficult and multiple-instance subsets.

The evaluation is broader than a standard benchmark-only study, including mixed-dataset training, zero-shot tests, cross-dataset transfer, synthetic language variations, camera-placement studies, representation comparisons, backbone scaling, runtime measurements, and component ablations.

The supplementary material gives useful implementation and efficiency details and tests a fully automated reconstruction variant. The authors also identify realistic failure modes involving ambiguous references, occlusion, and multipart objects.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, and the qualitative examples support the basic plausibility of the approach.
weaknesses: The key panorama-versus-pinhole experiment is insufficiently controlled or documented. The paper does not clearly state whether each pinhole configuration was separately trained, how its pixel/token budget and test-time augmentation compare with the panoramic model, or whether aggregation is identical. Consequently, Table 6 does not yet establish that panorama itself causes the large reported gain.

Several central claims are broader than the evidence. Cross-dataset evaluation uses ground-truth object segmentations, so it primarily measures candidate selection rather than end-to-end scene generalization. The text-robustness sets are generated by LLaMA without reported human validation, and affordance generation can encode the target category even after removing its noun.

The claimed practical input assumption is unclear. The full model requires not only a renderable scene but also calibrated original RGB views to construct the lifted semantic field. In the fully automated evaluation, COLMAP failures cause 49 of 141 validation scenes to be excluded, introducing substantial selection bias; the real-world demonstration contains only one scene and two queries.

There are unexplained numerical inconsistencies: the main paper reports the mesh model at 84.3/55.3/61.0 on ScanRefer, whereas Supplementary Table 1 reports 82.7/56.3/61.6. These differences affect the headline result and require reconciliation.

The ablation evidence for explicit geometry is weak. Adding geometry to the semantic-plus-EMD-plus-geometric-QA configuration improves only 60.7 to 61.0, and masking it at inference yields 60.5. No variance or repeated-run uncertainty is reported, so these small differences may be noise.

The proposed per-digit 'EMD' is not a faithful distance over the represented coordinate: independent place-weighted digit distances make numerically adjacent values across a carry boundary, such as 099 and 100, appear very far apart. This weakens the claimed numerical-distance interpretation, even if the auxiliary loss empirically helps.

Important reproducibility details remain missing, including the SAM variant and mask-selection procedure, outlier-removal thresholds, panorama seam handling for bounding boxes, exact adapter placement and dimensions, and fusion across yaw augmentations. No code or release commitment is stated.

Overall, the paper has a promising idea and strong reported results, but the central causal comparison and the generalization/practicality claims need tighter controls. I therefore lean only slightly toward acceptance rather than finding the current evidence fully convincing.

strengths: The central idea—using panoramic renderings as a 2D–3D interface for pretrained VLMs—is intuitive, original in this setting, and technically well motivated. A 360-degree view preserves substantially more relational context than ordinary pinhole images while avoiding a specialized 3D-language backbone.

The method is a coherent end-to-end system: structure-aware camera placement, aligned RGB/range/semantic features, lightweight adapters, and visibility-aware lifting collectively address important failure points in VLM-based 3D grounding.

The empirical results are strong. PanoGrounder reaches 74.6% overall on Nr3D and 61.0% Acc@0.25 on ScanRefer under single-dataset training, with particularly convincing gains on difficult distractor-heavy subsets. Joint training further improves these results.

The evaluation extends meaningfully beyond in-distribution benchmarks. Cross-dataset experiments on ARKitScenes and 3RScan, zero-shot comparison against much larger VLMs, and robustness tests involving paraphrases, affordances, and removed target nouns support the paper's generalization claims.

The panorama-versus-pinhole comparison is especially informative: the advantage grows as more contextual objects are mentioned, directly supporting the proposed representation rather than merely showing an aggregate benchmark improvement.

The supplementary experiments are unusually extensive. They examine camera placement, scene representation, adapter initialization and placement, test-time augmentation, backbone scaling, runtime, reconstruction noise, object categories, elevation, and failure cases. The self-captured RGB-only scene also provides useful evidence of feasibility outside curated benchmarks.
The presentation is clear and polished, with helpful diagrams, readable tables, detailed implementation information, and an appropriate limitations discussion.
weaknesses: The strongest main results rely on clean ScanNet meshes, known camera parameters, original RGB views for semantic-feature lifting, a 17B VLM, SAM, and about 9.6 VLM forward passes per query. Thus, the system is less lightweight and practical than the high-level framing may suggest. The automated reconstruction experiment covers only 92 of 141 validation scenes after excluding COLMAP failures and drops to 55.1% from 61.6%, while the real-world demonstration contains only one scene and two queries.

The cross-dataset generalization evaluation uses ground-truth object segmentations and therefore isolates instance-selection performance rather than evaluating the complete grounding pipeline. This is a reasonable controlled experiment, but it provides weaker support for end-to-end scene generalization than some of the surrounding language implies.

Four yaw rotations of each equirectangular panorama produce a large improvement, from 54.8% to 61.0%, despite preserving essentially the same visual content. This exposes considerable sensitivity to panorama alignment or seam location. The manuscript does not sufficiently analyze seam-crossing targets, circular bounding boxes, or precisely explain how predictions from rotated copies are reconciled in the complete aggregation procedure.

The proposed 'EMD' objective is actually a sum of independent per-digit expected absolute errors with place-value weights, rather than an Earth Mover's Distance over the distribution of the full numeric coordinate. It does not properly model carries across digits—for example, nearby coordinates such as 099 and 100 can appear far apart under the digitwise formulation. Its empirical gain is useful but modest, so the theoretical characterization should be corrected or better justified.

Several comparisons remain imperfectly controlled. The headline method combines a substantially stronger pretrained VLM, additional semantic features derived from source RGB views, geometric QA, multiple cameras, and test-time rotations. Although the ablations are helpful, there is no complete matched-compute comparison showing how much of the advantage over 3D-specialized systems comes from the panoramic representation itself versus backbone pretraining and inference budget.

Reproducibility would benefit from random-seed variation or confidence intervals, exact evaluated sample counts for the cross-dataset and generated-text subsets, clearer checkpoint-selection details, and release commitments for generated query variants and rerun-baseline configurations. These omissions do not overturn the strong empirical case but make small reported differences harder to interpret.
